Unit 1 · Solutions

Concepts

ConceptConcentration terms — and which depend on temperature

TermDefinitionUnitChanges with T?
Molarity Mmoles of solute per litre of solutionmol L−1yes
Molality mmoles of solute per kg of solventmol kg−1no
Normality Ngram equivalents of solute per litre of solutioneq L−1yes
Mole fraction xnA/(nA+nB); xA+xB = 1noneno
ppmmass of solute per 106 g of solutionnoneno
mass %g of solute per 100 g of solutionnoneno

Molality and mole fraction contain only masses, so they do not change with temperature; molarity and normality contain a volume, which expands on heating, so they fall. Normality = molarity × n-factor (e.g. 1 M H2SO4 = 2 N).

ConceptHenry's law

The mass (mole fraction) of a gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid: p = KH x.

  • A larger KH means a less soluble gas; KH rises with temperature, so gases are less soluble in warm water (aquatic life prefers cold water).
  • Soda water is bottled under high CO2 pressure; the fizz on opening is the gas coming out as p falls.
  • Scuba divers: N2 dissolved at depth bubbles out on fast ascent (the bends); tanks use He-diluted air.
  • Climbers at altitude: low p(O2) → less O2 in blood (anoxia).

ConceptRaoult's law, ideal and non-ideal solutions

Volatile solute: pA = xApA°, pB = xBpB°, ptotal = pA+pB (Dalton). Non-volatile solute: only the solvent contributes, so the relative lowering (p° − p)/p° = xsolute (Raoult's law for non-volatile solutes).

IdealPositive deviationNegative deviation
A–B vs A–A, B–B forcesequalA–B weakerA–B stronger
ΔHmix, ΔVmixboth 0both > 0both < 0
vapour pressureobeys Raoulthigher than Raoultlower than Raoult
azeotropenoneminimum-boilingmaximum-boiling
examplesbenzene + toluene; n-hexane + n-heptaneethanol + water (95.6 % ethanol, 351 K); ethanol + acetone; CS2 + acetonechloroform + acetone (H-bond C–H…O); HNO3 + water (68 %, 393.5 K)

An azeotrope boils at constant temperature with liquid and vapour of the same composition, so it cannot be separated by fractional distillation. Chloroform + acetone is negative (new H-bond); ethanol + water is positive (H-bonds broken).

DiagramVapour pressure against composition

DiagramThe two kinds of azeotrope

ConceptColligative properties and the van't Hoff factor

Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their nature: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure. Each is multiplied by i for a solute that dissociates or associates.

CaseiDegreeObserved molar mass
non-electrolyte (urea, glucose, sucrose)1—= normal
dissociation into n ions (NaCl n=2, BaCl2, K2SO4 n=3, K4[Fe(CN)6] n=5)1 + (n−1)αα = (i−1)/(n−1)lower than normal
association into (A)n (acetic/benzoic acid, phenol in benzene: dimers)1 − α(1 − 1/n)α = (1−i)/(1 − 1/n) = 2(1−i) for dimershigher than normal (about double)

i = normal molar massobserved molar mass = observed colligative propertycalculated colligative property

Ranking questions: multiply molality by i. 0.1 m AlCl3 (i=4) > MgCl2 (3) > KCl (2) > urea (1) for ΔTf, ΔTb and π — and the freezing point is then in the REVERSE order (AlCl3 freezes lowest).

ConceptOsmosis and osmotic pressure

  • Osmosis: flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from the dilute to the concentrated side. Diffusion needs no membrane and both solute and solvent move.
  • Osmotic pressure π: the excess pressure that must be applied to the solution to stop osmosis. π = CRT = (n/V)RT (van't Hoff; it behaves like a gas law — Boyle: π ∝ C at fixed T; Charles: π ∝ T at fixed C; Avogadro: equal π ⇒ equal number of particles).
  • Membranes: natural — animal bladder, egg membrane, cell walls; chemical — copper ferrocyanide Cu2[Fe(CN)6].
  • Isotonic: same π (0.9 % NaCl = saline, isotonic with blood). Hypertonic: higher π — RBCs shrink (crenation; in plant cells, plasmolysis); raw mango in brine shrivels. Hypotonic: lower π — RBCs swell and burst; dried grapes swell in water; shelled egg in water swells, in strong NaCl it shrinks.
  • Reverse osmosis: a pressure greater than π applied on the solution side drives pure solvent OUT (desalination of sea water; cellulose-acetate membrane).
  • Osmotic pressure is the best method for macromolecules (proteins, polymers): it is measured at room temperature, is large even for dilute solutions, and uses molarity.

DiagramOsmosis and reverse osmosis

Derivations

DerivationRelative lowering of vapour pressure gives the molar mass

  1. For a non-volatile solute only the solvent vaporises: p = x1p°.
  2. p° − p = p°(1 − x1) = p°x2, so p° − pp° = x2 = n2n1 + n2.
  3. For a dilute solution n2 « n1: p° − pp° ≈ n2n1 = w2M1M2w1 ⇒ M2 = w2M1p°w1(p° − p).

DerivationElevation of boiling point: ΔTb = Kbm (derivation included in the syllabus)

  1. A solution boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. The solute lowers the vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed: the solution curve lies below the solvent curve on the p–T diagram.
  2. Near Tb° the two curves are parallel, so ΔTb ∝ Δp (the lowering of vapour pressure).
  3. By Raoult, Δp = p°x2, and p° is fixed (= 1 atm at Tb°), so ΔTb ∝ x2.
  4. Dilute: x2 ≈ n2/n1 = (w2/M2)/(w1/M1) = m × M1/1000, where m = 1000w2/(M2w1) is the molality.
  5. M1 is a constant for a given solvent, so ΔTb = Kbm; Kb (ebullioscopic constant) = elevation for a 1 molal solution, unit K kg mol−1.
  6. Hence M2 = 1000 Kb w2ΔTb w1 (w1 in grams). With dissociation or association: ΔTb = iKbm.

Kb = RM1Tb2/(1000 ΔvapH) — water 0.52, benzene 2.53 K kg mol−1.

DerivationDepression of freezing point: ΔTf = Kfm

  1. At the freezing point, solid solvent and liquid have the same vapour pressure. The solution's vapour pressure is lower, so its curve meets the solid's curve at a LOWER temperature Tf.
  2. For small changes ΔTf = Tf° − Tf ∝ Δp ∝ x2 ≈ n2/n1.
  3. As above n2/n1 = mM1/1000, so ΔTf = Kfm; Kf (cryoscopic constant) = depression for a 1 molal solution.
  4. M2 = 1000 Kf w2ΔTf w1; with association/dissociation ΔTf = iKfm.

Kf: water 1.86, benzene 5.12, acetic acid 3.9 K kg mol−1. Only ONE solvent data set is needed: Tf from Tb via ΔTf = ΔTb×Kf/Kb.

DiagramWhy the boiling point rises and the freezing point falls

DerivationOsmotic pressure gives the molar mass

  1. π = CRT with C = n2/V = w2/(M2V).
  2. M2 = w2RTπV (V in litres, R = 0.0821 L atm K−1 mol−1, π in atm); with i: π = iCRT.
  3. Show π is colligative: π = (n/V)RT depends only on the number of moles of particles per litre, not on what they are.

FormulaeSolutions — formula sheet

QuantityFormula
molalitym = 1000 w2M2 w1
Henryp = KHx
RLVPp° − pp° = i x2
boiling / freezingΔTb = iKbm   ΔTf = iKfm
osmotic pressureπ = iCRT = i w2RTM2V
van't Hoff factori = Mnormal/Mobserved
dissociation into nα = (i − 1)/(n − 1)
association into n-merα = (1 − i)/(1 − 1/n)

Worked numericals

Worked exampleMolar mass of a polymer from osmotic pressure

S-1. 2.50 g of a polymer dissolved to make 250 mL of solution has an osmotic pressure of 4.10 × 10−3 atm at 27 °C. Find its molar mass (R = 0.0821 L atm K−1 mol−1).

Show working
  1. Given: w = 2.50 g, V = 0.250 L, π = 4.10 × 10−3 atm, T = 300 K.
  2. M = wRTπV = 2.50 × 0.0821 × 3004.10 × 10−3 × 0.250.
  3. = 61.575 / 1.025 × 10−3.

Answer M = 60 073 g mol−1 (about 6.0 × 104)

Note Osmotic pressure, not ΔTf, is used for polymers: ΔTf here would be only ~10−4 K.

Worked exampleDegree of association of benzoic acid (NCERT; set twice verbatim)

S-2. 2 g of benzoic acid (C6H5COOH) dissolved in 25 g of benzene lowers the freezing point by 1.62 K. Kf for benzene = 4.9 K kg mol−1. Find the percentage association if the acid forms dimers.

Show working
  1. Mobs = 1000 Kf w2ΔTf w1 = 1000 × 4.9 × 21.62 × 25 = 241.98 g mol−1.
  2. Mnormal = 122 g mol−1; i = 122/241.98 = 0.504.
  3. 2A ⇌ A2: i = 1 − α/2, so α = 2(1 − i) = 2(1 − 0.504).

Answer Mobs = 241.98 g mol−1 ; i = 0.504 ; association = 99.2 %

Note CISCE's own 2026 specimen key heads this item "degree of dissociation" but computes association. It is association: the observed molar mass is about twice the normal one.

Worked exampleObserved molar mass and degree of dissociation of NaCl from ΔTb

S-3. 0.585 g of NaCl in 200 g of water boils at 373.051 K (pure water 373.000 K here; Kb = 0.52 K kg mol−1). Find the observed molar mass, i and the degree of dissociation.

Show working
  1. ΔTb (observed) = 0.051 K.
  2. Mobs = 1000 × 0.52 × 0.5850.051 × 200 = 29.82 g mol−1.
  3. i = 58.5/29.82 = 1.96; NaCl → Na+ + Cl−, n = 2: α = (i − 1)/(2 − 1).

Answer Mobs = 29.82 g mol−1 ; i = 1.96 ; α = 0.962 (96.2 %)

Worked exampleDegree of dissociation of BaCl2 (a CISCE favourite data set)

S-4. 12.48 g of BaCl2 in 1 kg of water boils at 373.0832 K. Kb = 0.52 K kg mol−1, Ba = 137.2, Cl = 35.5. Calculate the degree of dissociation.

Show working
  1. M(BaCl2) = 208.2; m = 12.48/208.2 = 0.05994 mol kg−1.
  2. ΔTb(calculated) = 0.52 × 0.05994 = 0.03117 K; observed = 0.0832 K.
  3. i = 0.0832/0.03117 = 2.669; BaCl2 gives n = 3 ions: α = (2.669 − 1)/2.

Answer i = 2.669 ; α = 0.835 (83.5 %)

Worked exampleMass of antifreeze needed

S-5. How much ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, M = 62) must be added to 4 kg of water to prevent it freezing at −6 °C? Kf = 1.86 K kg mol−1.

Show working
  1. ΔTf = 6 K; w2 = ΔTf × w1 × M21000 Kf = 6 × 4000 × 621000 × 1.86.

Answer w = 800 g of ethylene glycol

Worked exampleMole fraction and molality

S-6. 46 g of ethanol (M 46) is mixed with 162 g of water (M 18). Find the mole fraction of each and the molality of ethanol.

Show working
  1. n(ethanol) = 1 mol; n(water) = 9 mol.
  2. xethanol = 1/10; xwater = 9/10 (they add to 1).
  3. molality = 1 mol / 0.162 kg.

Answer xethanol = 0.1 ; xwater = 0.9 ; m = 6.17 mol kg−1

Worked exampleBoiling point and freezing point of the same solution

S-7. 6 g of urea (M 60) is dissolved in 200 g of water. Find the boiling and freezing points (Kb 0.52, Kf 1.86 K kg mol−1; water boils at 373.15 K and freezes at 273.15 K).

Show working
  1. m = (6/60)/0.200 = 0.5 mol kg−1.
  2. ΔTb = 0.52 × 0.5 = 0.26 K; ΔTf = 1.86 × 0.5 = 0.93 K.

Answer Tb = 373.41 K ; Tf = 272.22 K

Note Given only the boiling point: ΔTf = ΔTb × Kf/Kb = 0.26 × 1.86/0.52 = 0.93 K.

Worked exampleVapour pressure of a solution (Raoult)

S-8. 10 g of glucose (M 180) is dissolved in 90 g of water. The vapour pressure of water at that temperature is 32.8 mm Hg. Find the vapour pressure of the solution.

Show working
  1. n2 = 10/180 = 0.05556; n1 = 90/18 = 5.
  2. x1 = 5/5.05556 = 0.98901; p = x1p° = 0.98901 × 32.8.

Answer p = 32.44 mm Hg ; lowering = 0.36 mm Hg

Worked exampleSolution isotonic with blood

S-9. Blood has an osmotic pressure of 7.65 atm at 37 °C. How much glucose should be used per litre for an intravenous injection isotonic with blood?

Show working
  1. Isotonic ⇒ same π: C = π/RT = 7.65/(0.0821 × 310) = 0.3006 mol L−1.
  2. mass = 0.3006 × 180.

Answer C = 0.3006 mol L−1 ; 54.1 g of glucose per litre

Worked exampleHenry's law

S-10. KH for methane in benzene at 298 K is 4.27 × 105 mm Hg. Find the solubility (mole fraction) of methane in benzene at 298 K under 760 mm Hg.

Show working
  1. x = p/KH = 760 / 4.27 × 105.

Answer x = 1.78 × 10−3

Worked exampleOsmotic pressure of a salt solution

S-11. Find the osmotic pressure at 27 °C of a solution of 5.85 g NaCl per litre, assuming complete dissociation.

Show working
  1. C = 5.85/58.5 = 0.1 mol L−1; i = 2.
  2. π = iCRT = 2 × 0.1 × 0.0821 × 300.

Answer π = 4.926 atm

Worked examplevan't Hoff factor of a partly dissociated complex salt

S-12. K4[Fe(CN)6] is 25 % dissociated in a dilute solution. What is its van't Hoff factor?

Show working
  1. K4[Fe(CN)6] → 4K+ + [Fe(CN)6]4−: n = 5.
  2. i = 1 + (n − 1)α = 1 + 4 × 0.25.

Answer i = 2.0

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Using mass of solution instead of mass of solvent in molality.
  • Forgetting i for electrolytes, or using i > 1 for acetic/benzoic acid in benzene (they associate: i < 1).
  • Freezing-point order is the reverse of the ΔTf order.
  • V in π = CRT must be in litres when R = 0.0821; use R = 8.314 only with π in Pa and V in m3.
  • A larger KH means LOWER solubility.

Recall sheetSolutions — recall sheet

  • Molality, mole fraction, ppm: temperature-independent.
  • p = KHx; solubility of gases falls with T.
  • Positive deviation → minimum-boiling azeotrope (ethanol + water); negative → maximum-boiling (CHCl3 + acetone, HNO3 + water).
  • RLVP = x2; ΔTb = Kbm; ΔTf = Kfm; π = CRT; all × i.
  • Dissociation: i > 1, Mobs smaller; association: i < 1, Mobs larger.
  • αdiss = (i−1)/(n−1); αdimer = 2(1−i).
  • 0.9 % NaCl isotonic with blood; hypertonic → cells shrink; hypotonic → swell.
  • Reverse osmosis: P > π on the solution side; desalination.
  • Osmotic pressure for proteins/polymers (large, room temperature).
  • Kb(water) 0.52, Kf(water) 1.86, Kf(benzene) 5.12.

Unit 2 · Electrochemistry

Concepts

ConceptGalvanic and electrolytic cells

Galvanic (electrochemical) cellElectrolytic cell
energychemical → electricalelectrical → chemical
reactionspontaneous (ΔG < 0, Ecell > 0)non-spontaneous, driven by a source
anodeoxidation, negativeoxidation, positive
cathodereduction, positivereduction, negative
salt bridgeneedednot needed

Cell notation: anode on the left, single line = phase boundary, double line = salt bridge: Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s). E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (reduction potentials) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V for the Daniell cell.

Salt bridge (KCl/KNO3/NH4NO3 in agar): completes the circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral; removing it stops the current. An external opposing emf > 1.10 V makes the Daniell cell run backwards as an electrolytic cell (Zn deposits, Cu dissolves).

Current flows from cathode to anode in the outer circuit; electrons from anode (Zn) to cathode (Cu).

DiagramThe Daniell cell

DiagramIon flow through the salt bridge

ConceptStandard hydrogen electrode and the electrochemical series

SHE: platinised Pt dipped in 1 M H+, H2 at 1 bar bubbled over it, 298 K; E° = 0 by definition. Pt(s) | H2(g, 1 bar) | H+(1 M). Limitations: hard to keep H2 at 1 bar and [H+] at 1 M; Pt is poisoned by impurities; cannot be used in oxidising solutions. To measure E°(Zn2+/Zn), couple Zn|Zn2+(1 M) with SHE: the cell reads 0.76 V with Zn as anode, so E° = −0.76 V; for copper SHE is the anode and E°(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V.

Electrochemical series (standard reduction potentials): the lower (more negative) E°, the stronger the reducing agent. Li (−3.05) > K > Mg (−2.37) > Al (−1.66) > Zn (−0.76) > Fe (−0.44) > H (0) > Cu (+0.34) > Ag (+0.80) as reducing agents; F2 (+2.87) is the strongest oxidising agent.

  • A metal with E° < 0 liberates H2 from dilute acid (Mg, Zn yes; Cu, Ag no).
  • A metal displaces any metal below it: CuSO4 cannot be stored in a Zn pot (Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu, E° = +1.10 V) but can be stored in a silver vessel.
  • A copper spoon in AgNO3: Cu is oxidised, silver deposits (E° = 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V).
  • Feasibility: E°cell > 0 ⇔ ΔG° < 0 ⇔ K > 1.

Factors affecting electrode potential: nature of the metal, concentration of its ions (Nernst), temperature.

DiagramThe standard hydrogen electrode

ConceptConductance: specific, molar, equivalent

QuantityDefinitionUnit
resistance R = ρl/ARΩ
conductance G = 1/RS (= Ω−1)
conductivity κ = 1/ρ = G × (l/A)conductance of 1 cm3 of solutionS cm−1
cell constant G* = l/A = κRmeasured with a standard KCl solutioncm−1
molar conductivity Λm = 1000κ/Mconductance of all the ions from 1 molS cm2 mol−1
equivalent conductivity Λeq = 1000κ/Nfrom 1 gram equivalentS cm2 eq−1

Metallic vs electrolytic conduction: electrons vs ions; no chemical change vs decomposition at the electrodes; resistance rises with T vs falls with T (more ions, less viscosity).

On dilution κ decreases (fewer ions per cm3) but Λm increases (the volume holding 1 mol grows; for a strong electrolyte inter-ionic attraction falls, for a weak one the degree of ionisation rises).

Strong electrolyte (KCl)Weak electrolyte (CH3COOH)
Λm vs √Cnearly straight line: Λm = Λm° − A√C (Debye–Hückel–Onsager)steep curve rising sharply at low C
rise on dilutionsmall (about 1.5 times)large (about 25 times)
Λm°by extrapolating the line to C = 0cannot be extrapolated — use Kohlrausch

The 2-mark reason CISCE keeps setting: weak electrolytes show a steep rise because dilution increases their degree of ionisation.

DiagramMolar conductivity against √C

DiagramMeasuring conductivity: the cell constant

ConceptKohlrausch's law and its uses

Statement: at infinite dilution each ion makes a definite contribution to the molar conductivity of an electrolyte, independent of the other ion: Λm° = ν+λ°+ + ν−λ°−.

  • Λ° of a weak electrolyte from strong ones: Λ°(CH3COOH) = Λ°(CH3COONa) + Λ°(HCl) − Λ°(NaCl); Λ°(NH4OH) = Λ°(NH4Cl) + ½Λ°(Ba(OH)2) − ½Λ°(BaCl2).
  • Degree of dissociation α = Λm/Λm°, then Ka = Cα2/(1 − α).
  • Λ° of a salt from ionic values: Λ°(BaCl2) = λ°(Ba2+) + 2λ°(Cl−).

ConceptFaraday's laws

First law: mass deposited ∝ charge passed: w = ZIt, Z = electrochemical equivalent = mass deposited by 1 coulomb. Second law: for the same charge, masses deposited are proportional to equivalent weights: w1/w2 = E1/E2 (so cells in series share one charge).

1 faraday = charge on 1 mol of electrons = NAe = 6.022 × 1023 × 1.602 × 10−19 ≈ 96 500 C mol−1. It deposits one gram equivalent (E = M/n). Z = E/96 500.

Charge needed = nF per mole: Cu2+ → Cu 2F = 193 000 C; Al3+ → Al 3F; MnO4− → Mn2+ 5F; Cr2O72− → 2Cr3+ 6F.

Products of electrolysis: at the cathode the species with the higher reduction potential is discharged — for aqueous NaCl H2 (not Na); at the anode Cl2 (overvoltage of O2).

Derivations

DerivationNernst equation and ΔG = −nFE

  1. For Mn+ + ne− → M: E = E° − RTnF ln 1[Mn+] = E° − 2.303RTnF log 1[Mn+].
  2. At 298 K, 2.303RT/F = 2.303 × 8.314 × 298 / 96 500 = 0.0591 V.
  3. For a cell aA + bB → cC + dD: Ecell = E°cell − 0.0591n log [C]c[D]d[A]a[B]b (pure solids = 1).
  4. Electrical work done by the cell = charge × emf = nF × E. The maximum useful work equals the fall in Gibbs energy: ΔG = −nFEcell, and ΔG° = −nFE°cell.
  5. At equilibrium Ecell = 0 and Q = K: 0 = E° − (0.0591/n) log K ⇒ log K = nE°/0.0591; also ΔG° = −2.303RT log K.

Signs: E° > 0 → ΔG° < 0 → K > 1 → spontaneous.

DerivationRelation between κ, Λm and Λeq

  1. A solution of molarity M holds M moles in 1000 cm3, so 1 mol occupies V = 1000/M cm3.
  2. Picture this volume between electrodes 1 cm apart: its conductance is κ × V.
  3. So Λm = κ × 1000/M; likewise Λeq = κ × 1000/N and Λeq = Λm/n-factor.

Cells, batteries and corrosion

Lead storage, secondaryPb + SO42− → PbSO4 + 2e−; PbO2 + SO42− + 4H+ + 2e− → PbSO4 + 2H2O38 % H2SO4; density of acid falls on discharge; recharged by reversing
H2–O2 fuel cell2H2 + 4OH− → 4H2O + 4e−; O2 + 2H2O + 4e− → 4OH−continuous supply of reactants; ~70 % efficient, pollution-free, water as by-product (Apollo)
Rusting (corrosion)anode Fe → Fe2+ + 2e−; cathode O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O; then 4Fe2+ + O2 + 4H2O → 2Fe2O3 + 8H+needs water and O2; faster with salt/CO2; prevented by paint, galvanising, sacrificial Mg/Zn (cathodic protection of ships)

DiagramMercury cell

DiagramLead storage battery

DiagramHydrogen–oxygen fuel cell

DiagramCorrosion as an electrochemical cell

Worked numericals

Worked exampleNernst: emf of a Mg–Cu cell

E-1. Mg | Mg2+(0.1 M) || Cu2+(0.01 M) | Cu; E°cell = 2.71 V. Find Ecell at 298 K.

Show working
  1. Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu, n = 2.
  2. E = E° − 0.05912 log [Mg2+][Cu2+] = 2.71 − 0.02955 log 10.

Answer Ecell = 2.6805 V

Worked exampleNernst with n = 6 and squared/cubed terms

E-2. 2Cr(s) + 3Fe2+(0.01 M) → 2Cr3+(0.1 M) + 3Fe(s). E°(Cr3+/Cr) = −0.74 V, E°(Fe2+/Fe) = −0.44 V. Find Ecell.

Show working
  1. E°cell = −0.44 − (−0.74) = 0.30 V; 6 electrons transferred.
  2. Q = [Cr3+]2/[Fe2+]3 = (0.1)2/(0.01)3 = 104.
  3. E = 0.30 − (0.0591/6) × 4.

Answer Ecell = 0.2606 V

Worked exampleNernst with a squared ion term

E-3. Zn | Zn2+(0.001 M) || Ag+(0.1 M) | Ag; E°(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Ag+/Ag) = +0.80 V.

Show working
  1. Zn + 2Ag+ → Zn2+ + 2Ag; E° = 1.56 V, n = 2.
  2. Q = 0.001/(0.1)2 = 0.1; E = 1.56 − 0.02955 × log 0.1 = 1.56 + 0.02955.

Answer Ecell = 1.5896 V

Worked exampleΔG° and K of the Daniell cell

E-4. E° for the Daniell cell is 1.10 V. Calculate ΔG° and the equilibrium constant at 298 K.

Show working
  1. ΔG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96 500 × 1.10 = −212 300 J.
  2. log K = nE°/0.0591 = 2 × 1.10/0.0591 = 37.225; K = antilog 37.225.

Answer ΔG° = −212.3 kJ mol−1 ; K = 1.68 × 1037

Worked exampleMaximum work from a Zn–Sn cell

E-5. Zn | Zn2+ || Sn2+ | Sn; E°(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Sn2+/Sn) = −0.14 V. Find ΔG°. Is it spontaneous?

Show working
  1. E°cell = −0.14 − (−0.76) = 0.62 V.
  2. ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 0.62 = −119 660 J; negative, so spontaneous.

Answer ΔG° = −119.66 kJ mol−1 (maximum work 119.66 kJ)

Worked exampleFaraday's second law: three cells in series

E-6. A current of 2.0 A is passed through AgNO3, CuSO4 and ZnSO4 solutions in series until 2.16 g of silver is deposited. For how long did it flow, and what masses of Cu and Zn were deposited? (Ag 108, Cu 63.5, Zn 65.4)

Show working
  1. Ag+ + e− → Ag: charge = 2.16 × 96 500/108 = 1930 C; t = 1930/2.0 s.
  2. w(Cu)/w(Ag) = E(Cu)/E(Ag) = 31.75/108 ⇒ w(Cu) = 2.16 × 31.75/108.
  3. w(Zn) = 2.16 × 32.7/108.

Answer t = 965 s ; Cu = 0.635 g ; Zn = 0.654 g

Worked exampleAtomic mass from electrolysis

E-7. A current of 0.75 A for 25 minutes deposits 0.370 g of copper from CuSO4. Find the atomic mass of copper.

Show working
  1. Q = 0.75 × 25 × 60 = 1125 C.
  2. Cu2+ + 2e−: M = w × 2F/Q = 0.370 × 2 × 96 500/1125.

Answer atomic mass = 63.48

Worked exampleCharge for a reduction

E-8. How many coulombs reduce 1 mol of MnO4− to Mn2+? How many faradays for 500 mL of 0.5 M KMnO4?

Show working
  1. Mn: +7 → +2, 5 electrons per ion: 5 × 96 500 C.
  2. moles = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25; faradays = 0.25 × 5.

Answer 482 500 C ; 1.25 F

Worked exampleKohlrausch: Λ° of acetic acid

E-9. Λ°(HCl) = 425.9, Λ°(NaCl) = 126.4, Λ°(CH3COONa) = 91.0 S cm2 mol−1. Find Λ°(CH3COOH).

Show working
  1. Λ°(CH3COOH) = λ(H+) + λ(CH3COO−) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH3COONa) − Λ°(NaCl).
  2. = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4.

Answer Λ° = 390.5 S cm2 mol−1

Worked exampleDegree of dissociation and Ka from conductivity (NCERT)

E-10. The conductivity of 0.001028 M acetic acid is 4.95 × 10−5 S cm−1; Λ° = 390.5 S cm2 mol−1. Find α and Ka.

Show working
  1. Λm = 1000κ/M = 1000 × 4.95 × 10−5/0.001028 = 48.15 S cm2 mol−1.
  2. α = 48.15/390.5 = 0.1233.
  3. Ka = Cα2/(1 − α) = 0.001028 × 0.12332/0.8767.

Answer Λm = 48.15 S cm2 mol−1 ; α = 0.1233 ; Ka = 1.78 × 10−5 mol L−1

Worked exampleCell constant, conductivity and molar conductivity

E-11. A cell filled with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm−1) has a resistance of 200 Ω. Filled with 0.02 M NaCl it reads 1100 Ω. Find the cell constant, and κ and Λm of the NaCl solution.

Show working
  1. G* = κR = 0.0129 × 200 = 2.58 cm−1.
  2. κ(NaCl) = G*/R = 2.58/1100 = 2.345 × 10−3 S cm−1.
  3. Λm = 1000 × 2.345 × 10−3/0.02.

Answer G* = 2.58 cm−1 ; κ = 2.345 × 10−3 S cm−1 ; Λm = 117.3 S cm2 mol−1

Worked exampleΛ° of salts from ionic conductivities

E-12. λ°: Ba2+ 127.2, Cl− 76.3, Al3+ 189, SO42− 160 S cm2 mol−1. Find Λ° of BaCl2 and Al2(SO4)3.

Show working
  1. BaCl2: 127.2 + 2 × 76.3.
  2. Al2(SO4)3: 2 × 189 + 3 × 160.

Answer Λ°(BaCl2) = 279.8 ; Λ°(Al2(SO4)3) = 858 S cm2 mol−1

Worked exampleMolar and equivalent conductivity

E-13. 5 g of BaCl2 (M 208.2) in 1000 cm3 of solution has κ = 0.0058 S cm−1. Find Λm and Λeq.

Show working
  1. M = 5/208.2 = 0.02402 mol L−1; Λm = 1000 × 0.0058/0.02402.
  2. Ba2+ carries 2 charges: N = 2M, so Λeq = Λm/2.

Answer Λm = 241.5 S cm2 mol−1 ; Λeq = 120.8 S cm2 eq−1

Common errorsCommon errors

  • E° values are NOT multiplied by the stoichiometric coefficient (intensive property); n is.
  • In Nernst the log term is products over reactants; the solid metals do not appear.
  • Λm = 1000κ/M needs κ in S cm−1; the 1000 converts L to cm3.
  • Anode is negative in a galvanic cell but positive in an electrolytic cell.
  • ΔG in J: remember to divide by 1000 for kJ, and keep the minus sign.

Recall sheetElectrochemistry — recall sheet

  • E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; anode on the left.
  • E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q; log K = nE°/0.0591.
  • ΔG° = −nFE° = −2.303RT log K.
  • G* = l/A = κR; Λm = 1000κ/M; Λeq = 1000κ/N.
  • Dilution: κ falls, Λm rises (weak electrolytes steeply).
  • Kohlrausch: Λ° = sum of ionic λ°; α = Λm/Λ°; Ka = Cα2/(1−α).
  • w = ZIt; 1 F = 96 500 C = NAe; Z is the mass per coulomb.
  • Series cells: w1/w2 = E1/E2.
  • Lower E° = stronger reductant; E° < 0 metals liberate H2.
  • Dry cell 1.5 V, mercury 1.35 V (constant), lead 2 V/cell, fuel cell H2–O2.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Faraday's laws: mass/time/atomic mass, cells in series (E-6, E-7) tier A, every board 2023-26
  • Nernst emf of a concentration cell (E-1 to E-3); ΔG° / maximum work (E-4, E-5) tier A
  • Kohlrausch: Λ° of a weak electrolyte by combining three others (E-9) tier A, specimen repeats
  • α = Λm/Λ° and Ka (E-10) tier A
  • Electrochemical-series reasoning: reducing power order, CuSO4 in a Zn pot, H2 liberation tier A, specimen Q2 + AR
  • Fill-in: Z (1 C) vs 96 500 C; anode from the sign of E° tier B, specimen 1A
  • κ and Λm on dilution; strong vs weak (1.5× vs 25×) tier B
  • Salt bridge, batteries, corrosion; cell constant numerical (E-11) tier C

Unit 3 · Chemical Kinetics

Concepts

ConceptRate of reaction

For aA + bB → cC + dD: rate = −1ad[A]dt = −1bd[B]dt = +1cd[C]dt = +1dd[D]dt. Unit mol L−1 s−1.

  • Average rate = −Δ[R]/Δt over an interval (slope of the chord); instantaneous rate = slope of the tangent to the [R]–t curve at that instant.
  • Factors: concentration, temperature (rate roughly doubles per 10 K), catalyst (lowers Ea by an alternative path, does not change ΔH or the equilibrium), surface area (powdered reacts faster), nature of reactants (ionic reactions fast; covalent bond-breaking slow), radiation (photochemical H2 + Cl2).
  • Law of mass action: rate ∝ product of active masses (molar concentrations) each raised to its coefficient — true only for an elementary step.

DiagramAverage and instantaneous rate

ConceptRate law, order and molecularity

Rate = k[A]x[B]y: order = x + y, found by experiment, may be 0, fractional or negative. k = rate constant = rate when all concentrations are 1 M; depends on T, not on concentration.

OrderMolecularity
sum of powers in the experimental rate lawnumber of species colliding in an elementary step
experimental; can be 0, fractional, negativetheoretical; whole number 1, 2 or 3 (never 0)
for the overall reactionfor each elementary step; meaningless for a complex reaction
e.g. H2 + Cl2 (photochemical) zero ordere.g. 2HI → H2 + I2 bimolecular

Pseudo-first-order: a bimolecular reaction in which one reactant is in large excess, so its concentration hardly changes: acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (excess) → CH3COOH + C2H5OH; inversion of cane sugar. Rate = k′[ester].

OrderUnits of kExample
0mol L−1 s−1 (same as rate)2NH3 → N2 + 3H2 on hot Pt; decomposition of HI on gold
1s−1radioactive decay; N2O5 decomposition; H2O2 decomposition
2L mol−1 s−12NO2 → 2NO + O2
n(mol L−1)1−n s−1

Mechanism: the slowest elementary step fixes the rate law. 2NO2 + F2 → 2NO2F with slow step NO2 + F2 → NO2F + F gives rate = k[NO2][F2].

ConceptActivation energy, collision theory and catalysis

  • Threshold energy: minimum energy colliding molecules must have to react. Activation energy Ea = threshold energy − average energy of the reactants. The activated complex at the top of the barrier is unstable, of high energy, and breaks into products or back into reactants.
  • Collision theory: molecules must collide; a collision is effective only if the energy is ≥ threshold AND the orientation is proper. Rate = ZABe−Ea/RT × P (steric factor).
  • Raising T by 10 K raises the fraction of molecules with E ≥ Ea (the Maxwell–Boltzmann tail) roughly two-fold, which is why the rate doubles; the collision frequency rises only a few per cent.
  • A catalyst provides a path of lower Ea; the same ΔH; it speeds forward and backward reactions equally.
  • Exothermic: products below reactants (ΔH < 0); endothermic: products above.

DiagramEnergy profile with and without a catalyst

DiagramEffective and ineffective collisions

DiagramMaxwell–Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures

Derivations

DerivationZero-order integrated rate law and half-life

  1. Rate = −d[R]/dt = k[R]0 = k ⇒ d[R] = −k dt.
  2. Integrate: [R] = −kt + I; at t = 0, [R] = [R]0, so [R] = [R]0 − kt, i.e. k = ([R]0 − [R])/t.
  3. Plot of [R] against t is a straight line of slope −k.
  4. Half-life: [R] = [R]0/2 ⇒ t½ = [R]0/2k — proportional to the initial concentration.

DerivationFirst-order integrated rate law (derivation required by the syllabus)

  1. Rate = −d[R]/dt = k[R] ⇒ d[R]/[R] = −k dt.
  2. Integrate: ln[R] = −kt + I; at t = 0, I = ln[R]0.
  3. ln[R] = ln[R]0 − kt, i.e. k = 2.303t log [R]0[R] = 2.303t log aa − x.
  4. Exponential form: [R] = [R]0e−kt. Plot of log[R] against t is linear, slope −k/2.303.
  5. Unit: k = (1/t) × (ratio) ⇒ time−1 (s−1), independent of the concentration unit.

DerivationFirst-order half-life is independent of the initial concentration

  1. Put [R] = [R]0/2 in k = (2.303/t) log([R]0/[R]).
  2. k = (2.303/t½) log 2 = (2.303 × 0.3010)/t½.
  3. t½ = 0.693/k — no [R]0 in it: the time to halve is the same whatever the amount present.

So after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)n: 3 half-lives → 12.5 % left (87.5 % reacted).

DerivationShow that t99% = 2 t90% and t75% = 2 t50%

  1. t99% = (2.303/k) log(100/1) = (2.303/k) × 2.
  2. t90% = (2.303/k) log(100/10) = (2.303/k) × 1. Ratio = 2.
  3. t75% = (2.303/k) log 4 = 2 × (2.303/k) log 2 = 2 t½.

DiagramEvery half-life halves what is left

DiagramThe integrated rate laws as graphs

DiagramHalf-life against initial concentration

DiagramOrder from a graph: zero order

DiagramOrder from a graph: first order

DerivationArrhenius equation and the two-temperature form

  1. k = Ae−Ea/RT: A = frequency (pre-exponential) factor; e−Ea/RT = fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea. As T → ∞, k → A.
  2. Log form: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, or log k = log A − Ea2.303R × 1T.
  3. Plot log k against 1/T: straight line, slope = −Ea/2.303R, intercept log A.
  4. Write it at T1 and T2 and subtract: log k2k1 = Ea2.303R (T2 − T1T1T2).

DiagramArrhenius plot

Worked numericals

Worked exampleFirst-order rate constant and half-life

K-1. In a first-order reaction the concentration falls from 0.8 M to 0.1 M in 30 minutes. Find k and t½.

Show working
  1. k = (2.303/30) log(0.8/0.1) = (2.303/30) log 8 = (2.303/30) × 0.9031.
  2. t½ = 0.693/k.

Answer k = 0.0693 min−1 ; t½ = 10.0 min

Note Quicker: 0.8 → 0.1 is three halvings, so 30 min = 3 t½.

Worked exampleTime for 90 % from the time for 40 %

K-2. A first-order reaction is 40 % complete in 20 minutes. How long will it take to be 90 % complete?

Show working
  1. k = (2.303/20) log(100/60) = (2.303/20) × 0.2218 = 0.02554 min−1.
  2. t90% = (2.303/k) log(100/10) = 2.303/0.02554.

Answer k = 0.02554 min−1 ; t = 90.2 min

Worked exampleRadioactive decay as first order (I-131)

K-3. The half-life of iodine-131 used for thyroid treatment is 8 days. What fraction of a dose remains after 32 days?

Show working
  1. 32 days = 4 half-lives; fraction left = (1/2)4.

Answer 1/16 = 0.0625 (6.25 %)

Worked exampleAge from carbon-14 (NCERT)

K-4. Wood from an archaeological site has 80 % of the 14C activity of fresh wood. t½(14C) = 5730 years. Estimate its age.

Show working
  1. k = 0.693/5730 = 1.209 × 10−4 y−1.
  2. t = (2.303/k) log(100/80) = (2.303 × 5730/0.693) × 0.0969.

Answer t ≈ 1845 years

Worked exampleEa when the rate doubles for a 10 K rise (NCERT; in every specimen 2024–27)

K-5. The rate of a reaction doubles when the temperature is raised from 298 K to 308 K. Calculate Ea.

Show working
  1. log 2 = Ea2.303 × 8.314 (10298 × 308).
  2. Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 0.3010 × 298 × 308/10 J mol−1.

Answer Ea = 52.9 kJ mol−1

Worked exampleThe same for 295 K → 305 K (2027 specimen Q10)

K-6. The rate of a reaction doubles from 295 K to 305 K. Find Ea.

Show working
  1. Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 0.3010 × 295 × 305/10 = 51 855 J mol−1.

Answer Ea = 51.86 kJ mol−1

Note CISCE's 2027 specimen key prints 151.85 kJ mol−1 and the unit J K−1 mol−1. Both are slips: the expression in its own working, 0.3010 × 19.147 × 295 × 305/10, evaluates to 51 855 J mol−1.

Worked exampleEa from two rate constants

K-7. k = 0.02 s−1 at 500 K and 0.07 s−1 at 700 K. Calculate Ea.

Show working
  1. log(0.07/0.02) = log 3.5 = 0.5441.
  2. Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 0.5441 × (500 × 700)/(700 − 500).

Answer Ea = 18.23 kJ mol−1

Worked exampleEa from the slope of an Arrhenius plot

K-8. A plot of log k against 1/T has slope −4621 K. Find Ea.

Show working
  1. slope = −Ea/2.303R ⇒ Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 4621.

Answer Ea = 88.48 kJ mol−1

Note If the plot is of ln k (not log k), Ea = −slope × R, with no 2.303.

Worked exampleRate law from an initial-rate table

K-9. For A + B → products:

Run[A] / M[B] / Minitial rate / mol L−1 s−1
10.10.12.0 × 10−3
20.20.14.0 × 10−3
30.10.28.0 × 10−3
Find the orders, the rate law, k and the rate when [A] = 0.3 M and [B] = 0.4 M.

Show working
  1. Runs 1, 2: [A] doubled, rate doubled ⇒ first order in A.
  2. Runs 1, 3: [B] doubled, rate × 4 ⇒ second order in B. Rate = k[A][B]2, overall order 3.
  3. k = 2.0 × 10−3/(0.1 × 0.12) = 2.0 mol−2 L2 s−1.
  4. Rate = 2.0 × 0.3 × 0.42.

Answer k = 2.0 mol−2 L2 s−1 ; rate = 0.096 mol L−1 s−1

Worked exampleZero-order half-life

K-10. A zero-order reaction has k = 2.5 × 10−3 mol L−1 s−1 and [R]0 = 0.50 M. Find t½ and the time for complete reaction.

Show working
  1. t½ = [R]0/2k = 0.50/(2 × 2.5 × 10−3).
  2. complete when [R] = 0: t = [R]0/k.

Answer t½ = 100 s ; t = 200 s

Worked exampleOverall order and units of k from a rate law

K-11. Give the overall order and units of k for (a) rate = k[A]½[B]3/2; (b) rate = k[A]3/2[B]−1.

Show working
  1. (a) order = ½ + 3/2 = 2; k units (mol L−1)1−2 s−1.
  2. (b) order = 3/2 − 1 = ½; k units (mol L−1)½ s−1.

Answer (a) order 2, L mol−1 s−1 ; (b) order ½, mol½ L−½ s−1

Worked exampleEffect of changing concentrations

K-12. Rate = k[A][B]2. By what factor does the rate change if (a) [B] is tripled; (b) both are doubled?

Show working
  1. (a) 32; (b) 2 × 22.

Answer (a) 9 times ; (b) 8 times

Worked examplePercentage reacted from half-life

K-13. The half-life of a first-order reaction is 30 min. How long does it take for 87.5 % to react?

Show working
  1. 87.5 % reacted = 12.5 % left = (1/2)3: three half-lives.

Answer t = 90 min

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Using log for ln (or the other way) — 2.303 goes with log10.
  • For "x % complete" the amount LEFT is (100 − x) %: log(100/(100 − x)).
  • Arrhenius: T in kelvin, R = 8.314 J K−1 mol−1, answer in J then kJ.
  • Molecularity is never zero or fractional; order can be.
  • Zero-order t½ depends on [R]0; first-order does not.

Recall sheetChemical kinetics — recall sheet

  • Rate = −(1/a)d[A]/dt; units mol L−1 s−1.
  • Zero order: [R] = [R]0 − kt; t½ = [R]0/2k; k has units of rate.
  • First order: k = (2.303/t) log([R]0/[R]); t½ = 0.693/k; unit s−1.
  • t75% = 2t½; t87.5% = 3t½; t99% = 2t90%.
  • k = Ae−Ea/RT; log(k2/k1) = (Ea/2.303R)(T2−T1)/(T1T2).
  • Slope of log k vs 1/T = −Ea/2.303R.
  • Doubling per 10 K near 300 K ↔ Ea ≈ 53 kJ mol−1.
  • Pseudo-first order: acid hydrolysis of ester, inversion of sugar.
  • Effective collision: energy ≥ threshold + proper orientation.
  • Catalyst lowers Ea; ΔH unchanged.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Ea from k (or t½) at two temperatures (K-7) and from doubling per 10 K (K-5, K-6) tier A, every board
  • Orders and rate law from an initial-rate table; new rate (K-9) tier A, specimen MCQ and C-section
  • First-order k, time for x % given y % (K-1, K-2) tier A, specimen Q13
  • Radioactive decay as first order: I-131, C-14 (K-3, K-4) tier A, specimen Q5
  • Overall order and units from fractional rate laws (K-11) tier A, specimen Q13(ii)
  • Half-life relations t75 = 2t50, t99 = 2t90, 87.5 % (K-13) tier B
  • Order vs molecularity, pseudo-first order; zero order k has the units of rate tier B/C
  • Arrhenius plot slope (K-8); energy profile with catalyst; collision theory tier C/D

Unit 4 · d- and f-Block Elements

Concepts

ConceptPosition, configuration and what counts as a transition element

d-Block: groups 3–12; general configuration (n−1)d1–10ns1–2. A transition element has an incompletely filled d-subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

  • Exceptions: Cr 3d54s1, Cu 3d104s1 — half-filled and filled d are extra stable (exchange energy, symmetry).
  • Zn, Cd, Hg are not transition elements: (n−1)d10 in the atom and in their only common ion M2+; they are also soft with low m.p. because the d electrons are all paired and take no part in metallic bonding.
  • Sc is transition (3d14s2) although Sc3+ is d0; Cu is transition because Cu2+ is 3d9.
  • Series: 3d Sc–Zn, 4d Y–Cd, 5d La, Hf–Hg, 6d Ac, Rf–Cn. 4f lanthanoids Ce–Lu, 5f actinoids Th–Lr.

ConceptTrends across the 3d series — with the reason for each

PropertyTrendReason
m.p., hardness, enthalpy of atomisationhigh; peak near the middle (V, Cr); Zn lowestmany unpaired d electrons → strong metallic bonding
atomic radiusfalls from Sc to Cr, then nearly constant, rises at Cu/Znnuclear charge rise balanced by shielding of added (n−1)d electrons
4d vs 5d radiusalmost equal (Zr 160, Hf 159 pm)lanthanoid contraction
densityrises Ti → Cumass up, volume down
ionisation enthalpyrises slowly and irregularlyd electrons shield the 4s poorly but steadily
IE1: Zn > CrZn 3d104s2 removes from a full stable 4s2; Cr loses 4s1 to give stable 3d5
IE2: Cr, Cu highCr+ 3d5, Cu+ 3d10 are stable configurations
IE3: Mn highMn2+ 3d5 is half-filled
oxidation statesmany, differing by 1; maximum at Mn (+7)(n−1)d and ns energies close; all can be used for bonding
colourcoloured ions if d1–d9d–d transition absorbs visible light; the complementary colour is seen
magnetismparamagnetic if unpaired e−; μ = √(n(n+2)) BMspin of unpaired electrons
catalysisFe (Haber), V2O5 (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), MnO2variable oxidation states; surface adsorption; complex formation
complexesreadily formedsmall, highly charged ions; vacant d orbitals of suitable energy
interstitial compoundsTiC, Mn4N, Fe3H, TiH1.7; non-stoichiometric, hard, high m.p., conductingsmall H, C, N, B atoms fit in holes of the metal lattice
alloysbrass (Cu–Zn), bronze (Cu–Sn), stainless steelsimilar atomic radii, so one atom substitutes for another

DiagramOxidation states of the 3d series

Concept"Give reasons" — the answers CISCE accepts

  • Cu2+ is coloured and paramagnetic, Cu+ colourless and diamagnetic: Cu2+ 3d9 has one unpaired electron (d–d transition possible); Cu+ 3d10 has none.
  • Ti3+ coloured, Ti4+ colourless: 3d1 vs 3d0. Zn2+ (ZnSO4) white: 3d10.
  • Co is attracted by a magnet, Zn is not: Co 3d74s2 has 3 unpaired electrons; Zn has none.
  • Mn2+ is the most paramagnetic divalent 3d ion: 3d5, five unpaired electrons, μ = 5.92 BM.
  • Mn2+ is more stable than Fe2+ towards oxidation: Mn2+ is already the stable half-filled d5; Fe2+ (d6) becomes the stable d5 Fe3+ on losing one electron.
  • Transition metals form alloys: similar atomic sizes let atoms replace one another in the lattice.
  • They act as catalysts: variable oxidation states let them form unstable intermediates; they adsorb reactants on their surface.
  • They form complexes: small size, high charge, vacant d orbitals to accept lone pairs.
  • Highest oxidation states appear in oxides and fluorides (Mn2O7, CrO3, VF5): O and F are small and highly electronegative; O also forms multiple bonds.
  • Cu+ disproportionates in water: the very high hydration enthalpy of Cu2+ more than repays the second IE.
  • Zr and Hf have almost identical properties: lanthanoid contraction makes their radii nearly equal.
  • La(OH)3 is more basic than Lu(OH)3: as Ln3+ shrinks, the M–OH bond becomes more covalent.

A reason earns its mark only when it names the configuration (d5, d10, unpaired electrons) — say it explicitly.

ConceptUsing them in titration

  • KMnO4 is its own indicator: the first permanent pink marks the end point. Acidify with dilute H2SO4 only — HCl is oxidised to Cl2, HNO3 is itself an oxidant.
  • Oxalic acid titration is done at 333 K; the first drops decolourise slowly, then quickly (Mn2+ is an autocatalyst).
  • K2Cr2O7 is a primary standard (pure, non-hygroscopic); indicator diphenylamine.
  • Na2Cr2O7 is not used as a primary standard because it is hygroscopic.

Lanthanoids and actinoids

ConceptLanthanoids

  • Configuration [Xe]4f1–145d0–16s2; common state +3. Ce4+ (4f0) is an oxidant; Eu2+ (4f7) and Yb2+ (4f14) are reductants — each heads for the stable +3 state.
  • Lanthanoid contraction: steady decrease in atomic and Ln3+ radii from La to Lu, because 4f electrons shield one another poorly from the rising nuclear charge. Consequences: Zr/Hf, Nb/Ta, Mo/W pairs have nearly equal radii and occur together; basicity of Ln(OH)3 decreases La → Lu; small differences allow separation by ion exchange; 5d elements are denser.
  • Colour from f–f transitions; La3+ (4f0) and Lu3+ (4f14) colourless.
  • Chemical reactivity (like Ca early in the series, like Al later): burn in O2 → Ln2O3; with H2 on heating → hydrides; with halogens → LnX3; with S → Ln2S3; with N2 → LnN; with C at 2773 K → carbides LnC2; with water → Ln(OH)3 + H2; with dilute acid → H2.
  • Mischmetall (~95 % lanthanoids, 5 % Fe, traces of S, C, Ca, Al): lighter flints; Mg-mischmetall alloy for bullets and shells.

DiagramLanthanoid contraction

DiagramIts consequence: 4d and 5d radii almost equal

Worked exampleSpin-only magnetic moments

D-1. Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Mn2+, Fe2+, Cr3+ and Cu2+ (Z: Cr 24, Mn 25, Fe 26, Cu 29).

Show working
  1. Mn2+ 3d5: n = 5, μ = √35.
  2. Fe2+ 3d6: n = 4, μ = √24.
  3. Cr3+ 3d3: n = 3, μ = √15.
  4. Cu2+ 3d9: n = 1, μ = √3.

Answer Mn2+ 5.92 BM ; Fe2+ 4.90 BM ; Cr3+ 3.87 BM ; Cu2+ 1.73 BM

Worked exampleUnpaired electrons from μ

D-2. An M2+ ion of the 3d series has μ = 2.83 BM. How many unpaired electrons? Suggest the ion.

Show working
  1. n(n + 2) = 2.832 = 8 ⇒ n = 2.
  2. Two unpaired: 3d8 (Ni2+) or 3d2 (Ti2+, rare) — Ni2+.

Answer n = 2 unpaired electrons (Ni2+)

Worked exampleMass of KMnO4 for a titration

D-3. What mass of KMnO4 (M 158) is needed to oxidise 0.1 mol of oxalate ion in acid solution?

Show working
  1. 2MnO4− : 5C2O42−; moles KMnO4 = 0.1 × 2/5 = 0.04.
  2. mass = 0.04 × 158.

Answer 6.32 g of KMnO4

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Writing 3d before 4s when ionising: 4s electrons are lost FIRST (Fe2+ is 3d6, not 3d44s2).
  • Calling Zn a transition metal, or saying Zn2+ compounds are coloured.
  • Acidifying KMnO4 with HCl.
  • Unbalanced charge in ionic equations — always count charge on both sides.

Recall sheetd- and f-block — recall sheet

  • Cr 3d54s1, Cu 3d104s1; ions lose 4s first.
  • Zn, Cd, Hg: d10, not transition, soft, low m.p.
  • μ = √(n(n+2)): 1 → 1.73, 2 → 2.83, 3 → 3.87, 4 → 4.90, 5 → 5.92 BM.
  • Colour: d–d transition; d0, d10 colourless.
  • Mn shows +7 (max); stable d5: Mn2+, Fe3+.
  • MnO4− + 8H+ + 5e− → Mn2+; neutral: + 3e− → MnO2.
  • Cr2O72− + 14H+ + 6e− → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O (orange → green).
  • Chromate (yellow) ⇌ dichromate (orange) by pH.
  • Lanthanoid contraction: poor 4f shielding; Zr ≈ Hf; basicity falls La → Lu.
  • Actinoids: more oxidation states, all radioactive, bigger contraction.

Unit 5 · Coordination Compounds

Concepts

ConceptThe vocabulary

  • Complex / coordination compound: a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules (ligands) by coordinate bonds; it keeps its identity in solution. A double salt (Mohr's salt FeSO4(NH4)2SO4·6H2O, potash alum) dissociates completely into simple ions and gives all their tests; K4[Fe(CN)6] gives no Fe2+ test and is not poisonous like KCN.
  • Ligand: donor of a lone pair (Lewis base; the metal is the Lewis acid). Denticity: mono (Cl−, NH3, H2O, CO), bi (en = H2NCH2CH2NH2, ox2−), tri (dien), tetra (trien), penta, hexa (EDTA4−).
  • Chelate: a polydentate ligand bound through two or more atoms forms a ring; chelates are more stable (chelate effect).
  • Ambidentate: can bind through either of two atoms — NO2− (N, nitrito-N) / ONO− (O, nitrito-O); SCN− / NCS−; CN−/NC−.
  • Coordination number: number of donor ATOMS bound (so [Co(en)3]3+ has CN 6). Oxidation number: the charge the metal would carry if all ligands were removed with their electron pairs.
  • Homoleptic [Co(NH3)6]3+ (one kind of ligand) vs heteroleptic [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+.

DiagramChelation by ethane-1,2-diamine

ConceptWerner's theory

Metals show two valencies: primary (ionisable, = oxidation number, satisfied by anions, shown outside the bracket) and secondary (non-ionisable, = coordination number, satisfied by ligands, directed in space so it fixes the geometry).

Only chloride OUTSIDE the square bracket precipitates as AgCl; molar conductivity rises with the number of ions.

ConceptIUPAC naming — rules with examples

  • Cation first, then anion. Inside the sphere: ligands in alphabetical order (prefixes di, tri ignored), then the metal, then its oxidation state in Roman numerals.
  • Anionic ligands end in -o: chlorido, cyanido, hydroxido, oxalato, nitrito-N, thiocyanato-S; neutral keep their names except aqua, ammine, carbonyl, nitrosyl. Complex ligands take bis-, tris-: bis(ethane-1,2-diamine).
  • In an anionic complex the metal ends in -ate: ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate, plumbate, stannate; cobaltate, nickelate, platinate.

ConceptStereoisomerism

  • Geometrical: square planar MA2B2 ([Pt(NH3)2Cl2] cis and trans), MABCD (3 isomers); octahedral MA4B2 ([Co(NH3)4Cl2]+: cis violet, trans green), [M(AA)2B2] ([Co(en)2Cl2]+, [Pt(en)2Cl2]2+), MA3B3 (fac, mer). Tetrahedral complexes show NO geometrical isomerism (all positions adjacent).
  • Optical: non-superimposable mirror images; common in [M(AA)3] ([Co(en)3]3+) and cis-[M(AA)2B2] (cis-[Co(en)2Cl2]+ is optically active; the trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is not).
  • Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]: square planar, dsp2, diamagnetic; anticancer (binds DNA); the trans isomer is inactive.

Bonding: VBT and CFT

ConceptValence bond theory — the recipe

  1. Find the oxidation state and the d-electron count of the metal ion.
  2. Decide the ligand field: strong ligands (CN−, CO, en, NH3 with Co3+) pair up the d electrons; weak ones (F−, Cl−, H2O with most M2+) do not.
  3. Count the orbitals needed (CN 6 → 6, CN 4 → 4) and choose: (n−1)d free → d2sp3 inner orbital, low spin; only nd free → sp3d2 outer orbital, high spin; CN 4: dsp2 square planar or sp3 tetrahedral.
  4. Magnetism from the unpaired electrons left: μ = √(n(n+2)) BM.

[Cr(NH3)6]3+Cr3+3anyd2sp3octahedralinner33.87
[Fe(CN)6]3−Fe3+5strongd2sp3octahedralinner11.73
[Fe(H2O)6]3+Fe3+5weaksp3d2octahedralouter55.92
[Fe(CN)6]4−Fe2+6strongd2sp3octahedralinner00.00
[Ni(CN)4]2−Ni2+8strongdsp2square planarinner00.00
[NiCl4]2−Ni2+8weaksp3tetrahedral—22.83

Limitations of VBT: no explanation of colour, no quantitative magnetism (orbital contribution), cannot tell weak from strong ligands, no distinction for the Δ.

DiagramOrbital boxes for inner- and outer-orbital complexes

DiagramVBT boxes, CFT splitting and shape for every complex in the table

Each card: the metal ion's d electrons (arrows) and the ligand pairs (××) in the valence-bond boxes, the same electrons in the crystal-field levels, and the geometry. The two theories must agree on the number of unpaired electrons.

ConceptCrystal field theory

  • Ligands are point charges; the five d orbitals lose their degeneracy. Octahedral: eg (dz², dx²−y², pointing at the ligands) rise by 0.6Δo; t2g (dxy, dyz, dzx) fall by 0.4Δo.
  • Tetrahedral: order inverted (e below t2), Δt = (4/9)Δo — too small to force pairing, so tetrahedral complexes are always high spin.
  • d4–d7: if Δo < P (pairing energy) the 4th electron enters eg (high spin, t2g3eg1); if Δo > P it pairs in t2g (low spin, t2g4eg0).
  • Spectrochemical series (weak → strong): I− < Br− < SCN− < Cl− < S2− < F− < OH− < C2O42− < H2O < NCS− < EDTA4− < NH3 < en < CN− < CO.
  • Colour: an electron is promoted t2g → eg by absorbing light of energy Δo; the complementary colour is seen. [Ti(H2O)6]3+ absorbs ~498 nm and looks violet. Anhydrous CuSO4 is white (no ligand field, no splitting), CuSO4·5H2O blue. [Ni(H2O)6]2+ green turns blue/violet with en (stronger field, larger Δ, shorter λ absorbed).
  • CFSE = (−0.4x + 0.6y)Δo for t2gxegy, plus P for each extra pair formed.

DiagramOctahedral and tetrahedral splitting

DiagramHigh spin and low spin, d4 to d7

ConceptStability and importance

  • Stability constant: M + 4L ⇌ ML4, β4 = [ML4]/[M][L]4; larger β = more stable ([Cu(NH3)4]2+ log β 13.1). Stability rises with charge on the metal, basicity of the ligand and chelation.
  • Qualitative analysis: Ni2+ + dimethylglyoxime → red precipitate; Cu2+ deep blue [Cu(NH3)4]2+; Fe3+ + SCN− blood red.
  • Hardness of water: EDTA titration of Ca2+/Mg2+. Lead poisoning: EDTA chelates Pb. Cisplatin: cancer therapy.
  • Metallurgy: Ag and Au dissolved as [Ag(CN)2]−, [Au(CN)2]− and displaced by Zn; Mond process Ni + 4CO → [Ni(CO)4].
  • Biology: chlorophyll (Mg), haemoglobin (Fe), vitamin B12 (Co). Photography: hypo dissolves AgBr as [Ag(S2O3)2]3−.

Worked numericals

Worked exampleOxidation number and coordination number

C-1. Find the oxidation state and coordination number of the metal in (a) K3[Fe(C2O4)3]; (b) [Co(en)2Cl2]+; (c) [Pt(NH3)4Cl2]SO4. Give the sum ON + CN for (b).

Show working
  1. (a) 3(+1) + x + 3(−2) = 0 ⇒ x = +3; three bidentate oxalates ⇒ CN 6.
  2. (b) x + 0 + 2(−1) = +1 ⇒ x = +3; 2 en (4 N) + 2 Cl ⇒ CN 6; sum 9.
  3. (c) sulphate is −2, so the cation is +2: x + 0 − 2 = +2 ⇒ x = +4; CN 6.

Answer (a) Fe +3, CN 6 ; (b) Co +3, CN 6, sum = 9 ; (c) Pt +4, CN 6

Worked exampleMass of AgCl from a Werner complex

C-2. 0.1 mol of CoCl3·5NH3 is treated with excess AgNO3. What mass of AgCl (M 143.5) forms?

Show working
  1. [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2: two ionisable Cl− per formula unit ⇒ 0.2 mol AgCl.
  2. mass = 0.2 × 143.5.

Answer 28.7 g of AgCl

Worked exampleCFSE and magnetic moment

C-3. For a d6 ion give the CFSE and spin-only μ in (a) a weak field [CoF6]3−; (b) a strong field [Co(NH3)6]3+.

Show working
  1. (a) t2g4eg2: CFSE = (−0.4 × 4 + 0.6 × 2)Δo = −0.4Δo; 4 unpaired; μ = √24.
  2. (b) t2g6: CFSE = −2.4Δo + 2P; 0 unpaired; diamagnetic.

Answer (a) −0.4Δo, μ = 4.90 BM ; (b) −2.4Δo + 2P, μ = 0

Worked exampled5 with Δo < P (2027 specimen Q4(ii) pattern)

C-4. Write the configuration and CFSE of a d5 ion when Δo < P, and when Δo > P.

Show working
  1. Δo < P: t2g3eg2, CFSE = −1.2 + 1.2 = 0; 5 unpaired.
  2. Δo > P: t2g5, CFSE = −2.0Δo + 2P; 1 unpaired.

Answer weak field: CFSE = 0 ; strong field: −2.0Δo + 2P

Note CISCE's 2027 key conflates CFSE with Δo itself; they are different quantities — CFSE is a multiple of Δo.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • CN counts donor atoms, not ligands (en counts 2).
  • Alphabetical order ignores di/tri/bis: "ammine" before "chlorido".
  • Tetrahedral complexes: no geometrical isomers, always high spin.
  • [Ni(CO)4] is Ni(0), 3d10 after pairing: sp3, diamagnetic.
  • Only chloride outside the bracket gives AgCl.

Recall sheetCoordination compounds — recall sheet

  • Primary valency = ON (ionisable); secondary = CN (directional).
  • CoCl3·xNH3: x = 6, 5, 4, 3 → 3, 2, 1, 0 AgCl.
  • Ionisation isomers: test the free ion (AgNO3, BaCl2, brown ring).
  • Linkage: NO2/ONO, SCN/NCS. Hydrate: CrCl3·6H2O.
  • Optical: [Co(en)3]3+, cis-[Co(en)2Cl2]+.
  • d2sp3 inner/low spin; sp3d2 outer/high spin; dsp2 square planar; sp3 tetrahedral.
  • [Ni(CN)4]2− dsp2 diamagnetic; [NiCl4]2− sp3 paramagnetic.
  • eg +0.6Δo, t2g −0.4Δo; Δt = 4/9 Δo.
  • Strong field: CO > CN− > en > NH3 > H2O > F− > Cl− > I−.
  • EDTA hexadentate; cisplatin anticancer; DMG for Ni.

Unit 6 · Haloalkanes and Haloarenes

Concepts

ConceptClassification, naming and the C–X bond

  • Mono-, di-, tri-halo; 1°, 2°, 3° by the carbon bearing X; allylic (X on C next to C=C), benzylic (C6H5CH2X), vinylic (X on C=C) and aryl (X on the ring). gem-dihalides (both X on one C, alkylidene halides) vs vic-dihalides (adjacent C, alkylene dihalides).
  • Names: CH3CH2CH(Cl)CH3 2-chlorobutane (sec-butyl chloride); (CH3)3CBr 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide); CH2=CHCH2Br 3-bromoprop-1-ene (allyl bromide); CHCl3 trichloromethane; CH2Cl2 dichloromethane.
  • C–X bond: polar (Cδ+–Xδ−), so C is attacked by nucleophiles. Bond length C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I, bond enthalpy in the reverse order, so reactivity R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.
  • In haloarenes the C–X bond is shorter and stronger: the carbon is sp2 (more s character) and a lone pair of X is delocalised into the ring, giving the bond partial double-bond character.
  • Physical: b.p. rise with mass (RI > RBr > RCl) and fall with branching; denser than water; insoluble in water (cannot break its H-bonds) but soluble in organic solvents. p-Dichlorobenzene melts higher than o/m (symmetry, better packing).

Mechanisms

MechanismSN2 and SN1

SN2SN1
stepsone: Nu− attacks from the back as X− leaves; transition state with C half-bonded to bothtwo: slow ionisation to a carbocation, then fast attack by Nu−
rate lawrate = k[RX][Nu−] (second order)rate = k[RX] (first order)
reactivityCH3X > 1° > 2° > 3° (steric hindrance)3° > 2° > 1° > CH3X (carbocation stability); allyl and benzyl fast
stereochemistryinversion (Walden)racemisation (planar carbocation attacked from both faces)
favoured bystrong nucleophile, polar aprotic solventweak nucleophile, polar protic solvent (water, alcohol)

Example SN2: OH− + CH3Cl → [HO···CH3···Cl]− → CH3OH + Cl−. Example SN1: (CH3)3CBr → (CH3)3C+ + Br− (slow); (CH3)3C+ + OH− → (CH3)3COH (fast).

Optical rotation: 2-chlorobutane has a chiral C* and exists as (+) and (−) enantiomers; a 50:50 mixture (racemic) is optically inactive.

MechanismE2 and E1 (β-elimination)

  • E2: one step — the base removes a β-H while X leaves; rate = k[RX][B−]; strong base (alc. KOH), heat.
  • E1: slow ionisation to the carbocation, then loss of a β-H+; rate = k[RX]; 3° halides.
  • Saytzeff rule: the H is lost from the β-carbon with fewer H, giving the more substituted (more stable) alkene: 2-bromobutane → but-2-ene (major) + but-1-ene.
  • Substitution vs elimination: aqueous KOH (OH− as nucleophile) → alcohol; alcoholic KOH (RO−, strong base, heat) → alkene.

ConceptHaloarenes: low reactivity, and their reactions

  • Why aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution: resonance gives C–X partial double-bond character; sp2 C holds X more tightly; the phenyl cation is unstable (no SN1); the electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile (no back-side attack).
  • −Cl → −OH (Dow): C6H5Cl + NaOH, 623 K, 300 atm → C6H5ONa, then H+ → phenol. o/p-NO2 groups make it easy: p-nitrochlorobenzene reacts at 443 K; 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene with warm water (addition–elimination via a carbanion stabilised by NO2).
  • −Cl → −NH2: C6H5Cl + 2NH3 → C6H5NH2 + NH4Cl (Cu2O, 475 K, 60 atm).
  • Electrophilic substitution: Cl is deactivating (−I) but ortho/para-directing (+R): chlorination (Cl2/FeCl3) → o- and p-dichlorobenzene; nitration (conc HNO3 + conc H2SO4) → o- and p-chloronitrobenzene (p major); sulphonation (conc H2SO4) → p-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid.
  • Reduction to benzene: C6H5Cl + 2[H] → C6H6 + HCl (Ni–Al alloy/NaOH, or Na + ethanol).
  • Wurtz–Fittig: C6H5Cl + CH3Cl + 2Na → C6H5CH3 + 2NaCl (dry ether). Fittig: 2C6H5Cl + 2Na → C6H5–C6H5 (biphenyl) + 2NaCl.
  • Grignard: C6H5Br + Mg → C6H5MgBr (dry ether).

MechanismElectrophilic substitution in chlorobenzene (nitration)

  1. Electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 → NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4−.
  2. NO2+ attacks the ring (slow) at o/p positions: the arenium ion has a resonance form in which the positive charge sits on the C bearing Cl, where a lone pair of Cl stabilises it (chloronium form) — not possible for meta attack.
  3. HSO4− removes H+ (fast), restoring aromaticity → 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene (major) + 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene.

Deactivating but o/p-directing: the −I effect slows every position; the +R effect helps only o and p.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • KCN gives nitrile, AgCN isocyanide — the reverse is a classic slip.
  • Aqueous KOH → substitution; alcoholic KOH → elimination.
  • Wurtz with a 3° halide (tert-butyl bromide) gives an alkene, not an alkane.
  • Chlorobenzene is o/p directing although deactivating; never write m-nitro product.
  • SN1 → racemisation (not inversion).

Recall sheetHaloalkanes and haloarenes — recall sheet

  • Reactivity RI > RBr > RCl; SN2 1° > 2° > 3°; SN1 3° > 2° > 1°.
  • SOCl2 is best (SO2, HCl escape).
  • Finkelstein NaI/acetone; Swarts AgF; Hunsdiecker RCOOAg + Br2.
  • KCN → RCN; AgCN → RNC; KNO2 → RONO; AgNO2 → RNO2.
  • Saytzeff: more substituted alkene major.
  • Aryl C–X: partial double bond, sp2, unreactive; Dow 623 K, 300 atm.
  • Cl on the ring: deactivating, o/p directing.
  • Wurtz 2RX + 2Na; Fittig 2ArX + 2Na; Wurtz–Fittig ArX + RX + 2Na.
  • CHCl3 + O2 → COCl2; stored dark with 1 % ethanol.
  • Freons deplete ozone; DDT non-biodegradable.

Unit 7 · Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers

Concepts

ConceptClassification, structure and physical properties

  • Monohydric, dihydric (glycol), polyhydric (glycerol); 1° RCH2OH, 2° R2CHOH, 3° R3COH; allylic, benzylic.
  • O is sp3; C–O–H angle 108.9° in methanol. In phenol the C–O bond is shorter (sp2 C, partial double bond by resonance).
  • Boiling points: alcohols » ethers and hydrocarbons of similar mass (intermolecular H-bonding): ethanol 351 K vs methoxymethane 248 K (functional isomers C2H6O). Among isomers b.p. falls with branching: butan-1-ol > butan-2-ol > 2-methylpropan-2-ol (smaller surface area).
  • Solubility: lower alcohols and phenol dissolve by H-bonding with water; solubility falls as the hydrocarbon part grows. Ethers are fairly miscible (H-bond from water to the ether O) but cannot H-bond with each other, so b.p. are low.
  • o-Nitrophenol is steam-volatile (intramolecular H-bond); p-nitrophenol is not (intermolecular H-bonds, association).

Mechanisms

MechanismAcid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol

  1. Protonation (fast): C2H5–OH + H+ → C2H5–O+H2 (a good leaving group, water).
  2. Loss of water (slow, rate-determining): CH3CH2–O+H2 → CH3CH2+ + H2O.
  3. Loss of a β-proton (fast): CH3CH2+ → CH2=CH2 + H+ (catalyst regenerated).
  4. At 413 K with excess alcohol a second molecule attacks the protonated alcohol instead (SN2): C2H5OH + C2H5O+H2 → C2H5O+(H)C2H5 → C2H5OC2H5 + H+.

3° alcohols dehydrate easiest because the 3° carbocation (step 2) is the most stable.

MechanismAcid-catalysed esterification (Fischer)

  1. Protonation of the carbonyl O of the acid makes the carbonyl C more electrophilic: RC(=O)OH + H+ → RC(=O+H)OH.
  2. The alcohol O attacks the carbonyl C (nucleophilic addition) → tetrahedral intermediate RC(OH)2–O+(H)R′.
  3. Proton transfer to an −OH turns it into −O+H2.
  4. Loss of water, then loss of H+: RCOOR′ (ester) + H3O+.

Isotope labelling shows the O of the water comes from the ACID (acyl–oxygen fission): the alcohol keeps its O.

MechanismCleavage of ethers by HI

  • Protonation of the ether O, then I− attacks. With 1°/methyl groups it is SN2: I− attacks the smaller group — CH3OC2H5 + HI → CH3I + C2H5OH.
  • With a 3° group it is SN1: the stable 3° carbocation forms, so the tertiary iodide results — (CH3)3COCH3 + HI → (CH3)3CI + CH3OH (the 2027 specimen assertion–reason).
  • Anisole: C6H5OCH3 + HI → C6H5OH + CH3I — never iodobenzene (the aryl C–O bond has partial double-bond character).
  • Excess HI converts the alcohol too: C2H5OC2H5 + 2HI → 2C2H5I + H2O.

ConceptAcidity of phenol

Phenol is acidic (pKa 10) because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalising its negative charge over the ring; the alkoxide ion has no such resonance. So phenol > water > ethanol (ethanol pKa ~16). Phenol reacts with NaOH (alcohols do not) but not with NaHCO3 (carboxylic acids do).

acidityp-cresol<phenol<m-nitrophenol<p-nitrophenol<2,4-dinitrophenol<picric acid

−NO2 at o/p withdraws electrons by −R and −I and stabilises the phenoxide more; −CH3, −OCH3 (electron-releasing) destabilise it. Among alcohols, CF3CH2OH > CCl3CH2OH > CH3CH2OH (−I effect).

DiagramRing substitution of phenol

MechanismElectrophilic substitution in phenol (bromination)

  1. The −OH lone pair is delocalised into the ring (+R), raising the electron density at the o and p carbons.
  2. Br2 is polarised by the electron-rich ring; the π electrons attack Brδ+ and Br− leaves (slow).
  3. The arenium ion from o/p attack has a resonance form with the + charge on O (oxonium): every atom has an octet, so it forms fast.
  4. Loss of H+ restores the aromatic ring: 4-bromophenol (and 2-bromophenol).

No Lewis acid is needed: the ring is activated enough to polarise Br2 itself.

Worked numericals

Worked exampleBromine consumed by phenol

A-1. What mass of bromine reacts with 9.4 g of phenol in bromine water? (C 12, H 1, O 16, Br 80)

Show working
  1. C6H5OH + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr.
  2. n(phenol) = 9.4/94 = 0.1 mol; n(Br2) = 0.3 mol; mass = 0.3 × 160.

Answer 48 g of Br2

Worked exampleHydrogen from sodium and ethanol

A-2. What volume of H2 at STP is liberated when 4.6 g of ethanol reacts completely with sodium?

Show working
  1. 2C2H5OH + 2Na → 2C2H5ONa + H2.
  2. n(ethanol) = 4.6/46 = 0.1 mol ⇒ 0.05 mol H2; V = 0.05 × 22.4 L.

Answer 1.12 L of H2

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Williamson with a 3° halide gives an alkene — always put the bulky group on the alkoxide.
  • Methanol does not give the iodoform test; ethanol does.
  • Anisole + HI gives phenol + CH3I, not iodobenzene.
  • Phenol does not react with NaHCO3.
  • Temperatures: 443 K ethene, 413 K ether; Kolbe 400 K; Reimer–Tiemann 340 K.

Recall sheetAlcohols, phenols and ethers — recall sheet

  • b.p.: alcohol > ether (H-bond); 1° > 2° > 3° isomers.
  • Grignard: HCHO → 1°, RCHO → 2°, R2CO → 3°.
  • Hydroboration–oxidation: anti-Markovnikov alcohol.
  • Lucas: 3° instant, 2° 5 min, 1° none.
  • Dehydration: protonation → carbocation (slow) → alkene.
  • Phenol > water > ethanol; NO2 increases, CH3 decreases acidity.
  • Cumene → phenol + acetone; Dow 623 K; Kolbe → salicylic acid; R–T → salicylaldehyde.

  • HI on mixed ether: SN2 → iodide of smaller group; 3° → tertiary iodide.
  • Phenol 0.2 % antiseptic, 1 % disinfectant.

Unit 8 · Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids

Concepts

ConceptStructure, naming and reactivity of the carbonyl group

  • C=O: sp2 carbon, trigonal planar, 120°; polar (Cδ+=Oδ−) — C is attacked by nucleophiles, O by electrophiles.
  • Names: HCHO methanal (formaldehyde), CH3CHO ethanal (acetaldehyde), CH3COCH3 propanone (acetone), C6H5CHO benzaldehyde, C6H5COCH3 acetophenone, CH3CH=CHCHO but-2-enal (crotonaldehyde).
  • Nucleophilic addition reactivity: HCHO > CH3CHO > CH3COCH3: alkyl groups push electrons (+I) onto C and crowd it (steric). Aromatic aldehydes are less reactive than aliphatic: resonance with the ring reduces the positive charge on C (benzaldehyde < propanal).
  • b.p.: higher than hydrocarbons and ethers (dipole–dipole) but lower than alcohols (no H-bond between molecules). Lower members are water-soluble (H-bond with water).
  • α-Hydrogen is acidic: the carbanion (enolate) is resonance-stabilised by C=O. That is what allows aldol condensation and the haloform reaction.

DiagramWhy −CHO and −COOH direct meta

Mechanisms

MechanismNucleophilic addition (HCN, base-catalysed)

  1. Base generates the nucleophile: HCN + OH− → CN− + H2O.
  2. CN− attacks the carbonyl C (slow): the sp2 C becomes sp3 and the π electrons move onto O → tetrahedral alkoxide.
  3. The alkoxide takes H+ from HCN or water (fast) → cyanohydrin, regenerating CN−.

Rate is set by step 2, so anything that crowds C or feeds it electrons (alkyl groups, a phenyl ring) slows addition.

MechanismAldol condensation

  1. OH− removes an α-H: CH3CHO + OH− → −CH2CHO (enolate, resonance-stabilised) + H2O.
  2. The carbanion adds to the C=O of a second molecule → CH3CH(O−)CH2CHO.
  3. Protonation by water → CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO (aldol, 3-hydroxybutanal).
  4. On heating, loss of water gives the conjugated α,β-unsaturated aldehyde CH3CH=CHCHO.

HCHO and C6H5CHO have no α-H, so they cannot form the enolate: they undergo Cannizzaro instead.

MechanismCannizzaro reaction

  1. OH− adds to the C=O of one aldehyde → tetrahedral anion HC(O−)(OH)H.
  2. That anion transfers a hydride ion (H−) to the carbonyl C of a second aldehyde molecule (rate-determining).
  3. The first becomes the acid (then carboxylate); the second becomes the alkoxide, which takes H+ → alcohol.

One molecule oxidised, one reduced: disproportionation. In crossed Cannizzaro, HCHO (the more reactive) is the hydride donor.

DiagramIodoform test: which compounds give it

Carboxylic acids

ConceptAcidity of carboxylic acids

RCOOH ⇌ RCOO− + H+: the carboxylate ion is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures (charge shared equally by both O), so acids are stronger than phenols (whose phenoxide places charge on C atoms too). Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity, electron-releasing ones decrease it.

acidityCH3COOH<C6H5COOH<HCOOH<ClCH2COOH<Cl2CHCOOH<Cl3CCOOH<F3CCOOH
substituted benzoicp-CH3OC6H4COOH<p-CH3C6H4COOH<C6H5COOH<p-NO2C6H4COOH

FCH2COOH > ClCH2COOH (F more electronegative); the effect falls with distance (2-chlorobutanoic > 3-chloro > 4-chloro). b.p. of acids are higher than alcohols of similar mass: they exist as H-bonded dimers.

Worked numericals

Worked exampleMolecular formula from composition

L-1. An acid contains C 40.0 %, H 6.67 %, O 53.3 % and has molar mass 60 g mol−1. Find its molecular formula and name it.

Show working
  1. C 40.0/12 = 3.33; H 6.67/1 = 6.67; O 53.3/16 = 3.33 ⇒ ratio 1 : 2 : 1, empirical CH2O (30).
  2. n = 60/30 = 2 ⇒ C2H4O2; an acid ⇒ CH3COOH.

Answer n = 2: C2H4O2, ethanoic acid

Worked exampleSilver from Tollens' reagent

L-2. What mass of silver is deposited when 2.2 g of ethanal reacts completely with Tollens' reagent? (Ag 108)

Show working
  1. RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ → RCOO− + 2Ag: 2 mol Ag per mol aldehyde.
  2. n(CH3CHO) = 2.2/44 = 0.05 mol ⇒ 0.1 mol Ag = 0.1 × 108 g.

Answer 10.8 g of silver

Note HCHO is the exception: it can reduce twice (via formic acid), giving up to 4 Ag per HCHO.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Acetaldehyde DOES give iodoform, so iodoform cannot tell it from acetone — use Tollens/Fehling.
  • Cannizzaro needs NO α-H and CONC alkali; aldol needs α-H and DILUTE alkali.
  • The aldol from ethanal is 3-hydroxybutanal.
  • Benzaldehyde gives Tollens but not Fehling.
  • Grignard + CO2 adds one carbon; soda-lime decarboxylation removes one; Hofmann (unit 9) removes one.

Recall sheetAldehydes, ketones and acids — recall sheet

  • Reactivity HCHO > CH3CHO > CH3COCH3; aromatic < aliphatic.
  • Rosenmund Pd/BaSO4; Stephen SnCl2/HCl; Etard CrO2Cl2.
  • Clemmensen Zn-Hg/HCl; Wolff–Kishner NH2NH2/KOH.
  • Aldol: α-H, dil. NaOH → β-hydroxy aldehyde → enal.
  • Cannizzaro: no α-H, conc NaOH → alcohol + salt.
  • Benzoin: alc. KCN; Perkin: (CH3CO)2O + CH3COONa → cinnamic acid.
  • Tollens: all aldehydes (and HCOOH); Fehling: aliphatic aldehydes only.
  • Iodoform: CH3CO–, CH3CH(OH)–.
  • Acidity: EWG ↑; F3C > Cl3C > ClCH2 > HCOOH > C6H5COOH > CH3COOH.
  • HVZ Cl2/red P (α-chloro); Kolbe electrolysis → R–R; soda lime → RH.

Unit 9 · Organic Compounds containing Nitrogen

Concepts

ConceptAmines: classification, structure, physical properties

  • 1° RNH2, 2° R2NH, 3° R3N, quaternary salt R4N+X−; aliphatic vs aromatic (aniline C6H5NH2). Names: CH3CH2NH2 ethanamine; (CH3)2NH N-methylmethanamine; (C2H5)3N N,N-diethylethanamine; C6H5NHCH3 N-methylaniline.
  • N is sp3 with a lone pair: pyramidal, C–N–C about 108°. In aniline the lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring.
  • b.p.: 1° > 2° > 3° (3° has no N–H, so no H-bonding among its molecules). Amines boil LOWER than alcohols of similar mass: N is less electronegative than O, so N–H…N bonds are weaker.
  • Solubility: lower aliphatic amines dissolve in water (H-bond); aniline is only slightly soluble (large hydrophobic ring) but dissolves in HCl as the anilinium salt. Aniline darkens in air (oxidation).

ConceptBasic strength of amines

Amines are Lewis/Brønsted bases because of the lone pair on N: RNH2 + H2O ⇌ RNH3+ + OH−; larger Kb (smaller pKb) = stronger base.

in water (ethyl)C6H5NH2<NH3<C2H5NH2<(C2H5)3N<(C2H5)2NH
in water (methyl)C6H5NH2<NH3<(CH3)3N<CH3NH2<(CH3)2NH
gas phaseNH3<1°<2°<3°
substituted anilinesp-nitroaniline<aniline<p-toluidine<p-anisidine
  • In the gas phase only the +I effect of alkyl groups matters, so 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3.
  • In water, the cation is also stabilised by H-bonding with water (best for RNH3+, 3 H) and 3° amines are crowded (steric): the three effects together give the order above.
  • Aniline is a much weaker base than NH3 (pKb 9.38 vs 4.75): its lone pair is delocalised over the ring and the anilinium ion has fewer resonance structures than aniline.
  • Electron-releasing −CH3, −OCH3 raise basicity; electron-withdrawing −NO2 lowers it.
  • Methylamine is more basic than methanol (and than water) because N holds its lone pair less tightly than O.

Diazonium salts

ConceptBenzenediazonium chloride

  • Made by diazotisation: aniline + NaNO2 + HCl at 273–278 K. Used at once, in solution.
  • Arenediazonium salts are stable at low temperature because the positive charge is delocalised over the ring (resonance); alkyldiazonium salts decompose at once, releasing N2 (which is why ethylamine + HNO2 gives ethanol).
  • Importance: the −N2+ group can be replaced by F, Cl, Br, I, CN, OH, H, NO2 — groups that cannot be introduced directly (fluorobenzene, iodobenzene, benzonitrile, 1,3,5-tribromobenzene). Coupling gives azo dyes.

Coupling with aniline

DiagramThe coupling product

Mechanisms

MechanismAcylation of an amine (nucleophilic acyl substitution)

  1. The N lone pair attacks the carbonyl C of CH3COCl → tetrahedral intermediate.
  2. Cl− leaves, C=O re-forms; a base (pyridine) removes H+ from N → CH3CONHR, and pyridine·HCl.
  3. Pyridine drives the equilibrium right by removing HCl (which would otherwise protonate the amine).

MechanismHofmann bromamide degradation (outline)

  1. RCONH2 + Br2 + OH− → RCONHBr (N-bromoamide).
  2. OH− removes the second N–H; Br− leaves and R migrates from C to N → isocyanate R–N=C=O.
  3. Hydrolysis: RNCO + 2OH− → RNH2 + CO32−. The carbonyl C is lost as carbonate: one C fewer.

MechanismDiazotisation and coupling (outline)

  1. NaNO2 + HCl → HNO2; HNO2 + H+ → NO+ (nitrosonium) + H2O.
  2. ArNH2 attacks NO+ → ArNH–N=O → (tautomerise, lose water) → ArN2+.
  3. Coupling: ArN2+ is a weak electrophile, so it attacks only strongly activated rings (phenoxide, aniline), at the para position; H+ is lost.

Worked numericals

Worked exampleHofmann bromamide: mass of amine

N-1. What mass of ethylamine is obtained from 7.3 g of propanamide by the Hofmann reaction, assuming 100 % yield? (C 12, H 1, N 14, O 16)

Show working
  1. C2H5CONH2 (M 73) → C2H5NH2 (M 45), 1 : 1.
  2. n = 7.3/73 = 0.1 mol ⇒ 0.1 × 45 g.

Answer 4.5 g of ethylamine

Worked exampleNitrogen from a primary amine

N-2. What volume of N2 at STP is evolved when 4.5 g of ethylamine reacts completely with nitrous acid?

Show working
  1. C2H5NH2 + HNO2 → C2H5OH + N2 + H2O.
  2. n = 4.5/45 = 0.1 mol N2 = 0.1 × 22.4 L.

Answer 2.24 L of N2

Worked exampleBromination of aniline

N-3. What mass of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (M 330) forms from 9.3 g of aniline, and how much Br2 is used?

Show working
  1. n(aniline) = 9.3/93 = 0.1 mol ⇒ 0.1 mol product = 33 g.
  2. Br2: 0.3 mol × 160 g mol−1.

Answer 33 g of tribromoaniline ; 48 g of Br2

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Hofmann gives one C fewer; LiAlH4 reduction of an amide keeps the same number.
  • Carbylamine is for 1° amines only, and chloroform needs alcoholic KOH.
  • Aniline cannot be made by Gabriel synthesis.
  • Diazotisation must be at 273–278 K; above that the salt gives phenol.
  • Direct nitration of aniline gives a lot of m-nitroaniline.

Recall sheetNitrogen compounds — recall sheet

  • Basicity in water: 2° > 3° > 1° > NH3 > aniline (ethyl series); gas phase 3° > 2° > 1°.
  • b.p. 1° > 2° > 3°; amines < alcohols.
  • Hofmann: RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → RNH2 (C − 1).
  • RCN + LiAlH4 → 1° amine; RNC + LiAlH4 → 2° amine.
  • Carbylamine: RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH → RNC (1° only).
  • Hinsberg: 1° soluble in KOH, 2° insoluble, 3° no reaction.
  • 1° aliphatic + HNO2 → ROH + N2; aniline → diazonium at 273–278 K.
  • Sandmeyer Cu2X2; Gattermann Cu; Balz–Schiemann HBF4; H3PO2 → C6H6.
  • Coupling: phenol (alkaline) → orange p-hydroxyazobenzene; aniline → yellow p-aminoazobenzene.
  • Aniline + Br2(aq) → 2,4,6-tribromoaniline; no Friedel–Crafts.

Unit 10 · Biomolecules

Carbohydrates

ConceptDefinition and classification

  • Carbohydrates: optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give them on hydrolysis.
  • Monosaccharides (cannot be hydrolysed): glucose (aldohexose), fructose (ketohexose), ribose (aldopentose). Oligosaccharides (2–10 units): sucrose, maltose, lactose. Polysaccharides: starch, cellulose, glycogen.
  • Reducing sugars reduce Tollens'/Fehling's (free aldehyde or ketone group): all monosaccharides, maltose, lactose. Non-reducing: sucrose (both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond).
  • D/L: relative configuration, by comparison with glyceraldehyde — D if the −OH on the lowest asymmetric carbon points RIGHT in the Fischer projection. D/L is unrelated to the sign of rotation (+/−): D-fructose is laevorotatory.

ConceptGlucose: establishing the open-chain structure

ReactionProductWhat it proves
heat with HIn-hexanesix C in a straight chain
NH2OHoximeC=O present
HCNcyanohydrinC=O present
bromine water (mild oxidant)gluconic acid C6H12O7the C=O is an aldehyde
acetic anhydrideglucose pentaacetatefive −OH groups (on different C, since it is stable)
conc HNO3saccharic (glucaric) acida 1° alcohol group (C6) as well
excess phenylhydrazineglucosazone (3 mol used)C1 and C2 react; glucose and fructose give the SAME osazone

Bromine-water test: CH2OH(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O → CH2OH(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr — glucose decolourises bromine water, fructose (a ketose) does not. This is how the two are told apart.

DiagramD-glucose: Fischer projection

ConceptThe cyclic structure

  • Evidence against the open chain: glucose does not give Schiff's test or form a NaHSO3 adduct; the pentaacetate does not react with NH2OH; glucose exists in two crystalline forms.
  • The C5 −OH adds to the C1 aldehyde: a six-membered pyranose ring (hemiacetal). C1 becomes a new chiral centre: two anomers, α-D-glucose (C1–OH down, m.p. 419 K, [α] +111°) and β-D-glucose (C1–OH up, m.p. 423 K, +19.2°).
  • Mutarotation: in water either anomer changes to an equilibrium mixture of [α] +52.5° through the open-chain form.
  • Fructose forms a five-membered furanose ring (C5 −OH adds to the C2 ketone).

DiagramHaworth structures of the anomers

Glycosidic linkage: the ether (C–O–C) link between two sugar units, formed with loss of water.

Proteins

ConceptAmino acids

  • General formula H2N–CHR–COOH (α-amino acids). Glycine (R = H) is the only one NOT optically active; the rest are L-configured.
  • Essential (from the diet: valine, leucine, lysine…) vs non-essential (made in the body: glycine, alanine). Neutral, acidic (aspartic, glutamic acid: extra −COOH) and basic (lysine, arginine: extra −NH2).
  • Zwitterion: in water the −COOH gives its proton to −NH2: H3N+–CHR–COO− — so amino acids are amphoteric, crystalline, high-melting and water-soluble.
  • Isoelectric point: the pH at which the zwitterion carries no net charge and does not migrate in an electric field.

DiagramThe zwitterion

ConceptPeptide bond and protein structure

  • Peptide bond: −CO−NH− amide link from the −COOH of one amino acid and −NH2 of the next, with loss of water. Glycine + alanine → glycylalanine H2NCH2CONHCH(CH3)COOH (Gly-Ala). Dipeptide, tripeptide … polypeptide (> 10), protein (> 100 residues, M > 10 000).
  • Primary: the sequence of amino acids. Secondary: α-helix (right-handed, H-bond from −NH of one turn to C=O of the next) or β-pleated sheet (chains side by side). Tertiary: overall folding (H-bonds, disulphide, ionic, van der Waals) → fibrous or globular. Quaternary: arrangement of several subunits (haemoglobin, 4).
  • Fibrous (keratin in hair and wool, myosin in muscle, collagen): long parallel chains, insoluble. Globular (insulin, albumin, haemoglobin): spherical, water-soluble.
  • Denaturation: heat or change of pH disrupts the secondary and tertiary structure (H-bonds break) and biological activity is lost; the primary structure is unchanged. Boiling an egg coagulates the albumin; curdling of milk is caused by lactic acid from bacteria.

DiagramThe peptide bond

DiagramFour levels of protein structure

ConceptEnzymes and hormones (elementary)

  • Enzymes: globular-protein biocatalysts; highly specific, work at body temperature and pH, lower the activation energy; activity falls at high temperature (denaturation). Maltase: maltose → glucose; invertase: sucrose → glucose + fructose; zymase: glucose → ethanol.
  • Hormones: chemical messengers from endocrine glands — insulin (globular protein, lowers blood sugar), thyroxine (iodinated amino acid), adrenaline, steroid hormones (oestrogen, testosterone).

A, D, E, K are stored in the liver and fat tissue; B and C are water-soluble, excreted in urine, and must be taken regularly (B12 is the exception — it is stored). Chemical names and structures are NOT required.

ConceptNucleic acids

DNARNA

Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate. Complete hydrolysis of a nucleotide gives a base, a pentose and phosphoric acid. Purines: A, G; pyrimidines: C, T, U. (Structures are not examined, but they show why A pairs only with T and G only with C.)

Worked numericals

Worked exampleMolar mass of a dipeptide

B-1. Find the molar mass of glycylalanine (glycine 75, alanine 89 g mol−1). How many peptide bonds does a tripeptide have?

Show working
  1. Condensation loses one H2O (18): 75 + 89 − 18.
  2. n amino acids are joined by n − 1 peptide bonds.

Answer M(Gly-Ala) = 146 g mol−1 ; a tripeptide has 2 peptide bonds

Worked exampleGlucose pentaacetate

B-2. Glucose (M 180) is acetylated with acetic anhydride. What is the molar mass of the product, and how many −OH groups does the mass change prove?

Show working
  1. Each −OH → −OCOCH3 adds C2H2O = 42.
  2. observed 390 ⇒ (390 − 180)/42 = 5 groups.

Answer M = 390 g mol−1 ; 5 hydroxyl groups

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Sucrose is non-reducing although its hydrolysis products are reducing.
  • D/L is configuration, not the sign of rotation.
  • Denaturation leaves the primary structure intact.
  • Thymine is in DNA only; uracil in RNA only.
  • Glycine is optically inactive.

Recall sheetBiomolecules — recall sheet

  • Glucose: HI → n-hexane; Br2 water → gluconic acid (aldose); Ac2O → pentaacetate; HNO3 → saccharic acid; 3 mol PhNHNH2.
  • Pyranose ring; α/β anomers differ at C1; mutarotation to +52.5°.
  • Sucrose α1–β2, non-reducing, invert sugar; maltose α1–4; lactose β1–4.
  • Starch: amylose + amylopectin; cellulose β-1,4; glycogen animal starch.
  • Zwitterion, isoelectric point; glycine not chiral.
  • Peptide bond −CONH−; primary = sequence; α-helix, β-sheet.
  • Fibrous keratin/myosin; globular insulin/albumin.
  • Denaturation: boiled egg, curdled milk.
  • Fat-soluble A D E K; B, C water-soluble.
  • A – night blindness; C – scurvy; D – rickets; B1 – beriberi; B12 – pernicious anaemia; K – clotting.
  • DNA: deoxyribose, T, double helix; RNA: ribose, U.
